title: Message Queue / Event Streaming — Kafka vs RabbitMQ vs SQS: when to use each, at-least-once vs exactly-once delivery, consumer groups, dead letter queues.
shortTitle: Message Queue / Event Streaming — Kafka vs RabbitMQ vs SQS

s1_definition.profdef: A message queue or event streaming platform decouples producers from consumers by passing messages through an intermediary, enabling asynchronous processing, buffering, and scalability. RabbitMQ is a traditional message broker optimized for flexible routing and per-message acknowledgement; Amazon SQS is a fully managed queue for simple, reliable at-least-once delivery; Apache Kafka is a distributed, partitioned, durable log optimized for high-throughput event streaming and replay. Key concepts include delivery semantics, consumer groups for parallelism, and dead-letter queues for poison messages.
s1_definition.analogy: When Rajesh transfers money at National Bank of India, several things must follow: update the ledger, send a receipt, notify fraud monitoring. Instead of the transfer desk doing all of that while Rajesh waits, it drops a note in an internal mail system and moves on; other departments pick up their copies and act. That internal mail system is a message queue. RabbitMQ is like a smart mailroom that routes each letter to the right desk. SQS is a simple, reliable outbox managed by Amazon. Kafka is a permanent logbook many departments can read and re-read at their own pace.
s1_definition.oneliner: Decouple producers from consumers with a queue; pick RabbitMQ for routing, SQS for simple managed queues, Kafka for high-throughput replayable streams, and always plan delivery semantics and dead-letter handling.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A message queue or event streaming platform decouples producers from consumers by passing messages through an intermediary, enabling asynchronous processing, buffering, and scalability. RabbitMQ is a traditional message broker optimized for flexible routing and per-message acknowledgement; Amazon SQS is a fully managed queue for simple, reliable at-least-once delivery; Apache Kafka is a distributed, partitioned, durable log optimized for high-throughput event streaming and replay. Key concepts include delivery semantics, consumer groups for parallelism, and dead-letter queues for poison messages.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When Rajesh transfers money at National Bank of India, several things must follow: update the ledger, send a receipt, notify fraud monitoring. Instead of the transfer desk doing all of that while Rajesh waits, it drops a note in an internal mail system and moves on; other departments pick up their copies and act. That internal mail system is a message queue. RabbitMQ is like a smart mailroom that routes each letter to the right desk. SQS is a simple, reliable outbox managed by Amazon. Kafka is a permanent logbook many departments can read and re-read at their own pace.

**One line to remember:** Decouple producers from consumers with a queue; pick RabbitMQ for routing, SQS for simple managed queues, Kafka for high-throughput replayable streams, and always plan delivery semantics and dead-letter handling.

sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's transfer service used to synchronously update the ledger, send a receipt, and notify fraud, so a slow email server slowed transfers. The real problem is coupling a fast operation to slow side effects. This is exactly what a message queue decouples.

Problem 2 — a receipt message is occasionally redelivered because the queue guarantees at-least-once, and the bank must not send two receipts or process a transfer twice. The real problem is handling redelivery. This is exactly why consumers must be idempotent.

Problem 3 — one malformed event keeps failing and would otherwise jam the whole queue. The real problem is poison messages. This is exactly what a dead-letter queue handles.

We build a runnable messaging core: a partitioned `Topic`, a `Producer` keying by account, `ConsumerGroup` members sharing partitions, idempotent consumers, and a `DeadLetterQueue` after a retry limit. The demo produces transfer events, shows consumer-group parallelism and per-key ordering, deduplicates a redelivered event, and dead-letters a poison message.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is five transfer events, including a duplicate of the first and a poison message, into a topic with three partitions consumed by a group of two.

Step 1: The producer keys each event by account. Both SAV2001 events and the duplicate hash to the same partition, so they land in order on that one partition, while the CUR3001 event lands on a different partition. This is how per-key ordering is guaranteed.

Step 2: The consumer group assigns the three partitions across its two members round-robin, so each partition is owned by exactly one consumer, giving parallelism without processing any message twice within the group.

Step 3: The first SAV2001 message is processed and its id recorded. The later duplicate of that id is recognized by the idempotent consumer and skipped, so the transfer is not processed twice despite at-least-once delivery.

Step 4: The poison message throws on every attempt. After exceeding the retry limit, it is moved to the dead-letter queue rather than blocking the partition or being lost. The data that changed is the processed-id set and the dead-letter queue; the ordering within each partition is preserved throughout.

```

  [RETRY] ──exceeds limit──→ [DEAD_LETTER]

  1. group.consumeAll()
  2.   → partition p → owner consumer

    Pre:  consumer owns the partition
    Post: processed once (dedup); poison → DLQ after retries
    Ordering preserved within a partition
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A message queue or event streaming platform decouples producers from consumers through an intermediary, which enables asynchronous processing, buffering, and independent scaling. I always compare the three common choices by matching their guarantees to the problem. RabbitMQ is a traditional broker with exchanges and per-message acknowledgement, excellent when I need rich routing and moderate throughput. Amazon SQS is a fully managed queue that gives reliable at-least-once delivery with almost no operational burden, ideal when I just want a simple, dependable queue. Apache Kafka is a distributed, partitioned, durable log that retains messages for replay, which is the right choice for high-throughput event streaming, analytics pipelines, and letting many independent consumer groups read the same stream.

In the banking context at National Bank of India, this decoupling solved a real problem. The transfer service used to synchronously update the ledger, send a receipt, and notify fraud monitoring, so a slow email server slowed down every transfer. After publishing a transfer event to a topic and letting separate consumer groups handle the ledger, receipts, and fraud independently, the transfer returned immediately and each side effect proceeded at its own pace.

Two guarantees dominate my design thinking. The first is delivery semantics. At-least-once means a message can be redelivered, so I make consumers idempotent by recording a message id and skipping duplicates, which is simpler and more robust than chasing true exactly-once. Kafka can provide exactly-once within its own boundary using transactional producers, but I still design the consumer to be idempotent for safety. The second is consumer groups: a group shares a topic's partitions among its members so each message is processed once per group, and I scale parallelism by adding members up to the partition count.

The operational details I never skip are dead-letter queues and ordering. A dead-letter queue captures messages that repeatedly fail after a retry limit, so a single poison message does not jam the queue or vanish silently, and I can investigate it later. Ordering is guaranteed only per partition, so when I need strict ordering for a particular account I partition by account id, accepting that this limits parallelism for a very hot account. Choosing the platform by matching its delivery, ordering, and retention guarantees to the domain, rather than by fashion, is what makes an asynchronous banking system both fast and correct.
